nv_mount_charleston.blurb: Mount Charleston is a limestone climbing area in the Spring Mountains, northwest of Las Vegas. Its forested slopes are noticeably cooler than the desert floor, so it is mainly a summer and fall choice, and winter turns cold and snowy. Sport climbing dominates, with grades running from 5.10 to 5.14 and the bulk of the climbing in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, plus a harder tier above that. Smaller numbers of boulder problems, with winter ice and mixed lines, round it out. The rock changes character from wall to wall, from chert-banded stone to sharp, steep and chunky limestone, and most of it is technical face and overhanging climbing. The main pockets are Kyle Canyon, Route 158 and the Mount Charleston bouldering.

ca_pine_creek_canyon.blurb: Pine Creek Canyon is a big granite gorge above the town of Bishop in the Eastern Sierra, with so much rock that it is hard to take in at first. Sport routes are slightly more numerous than trad, and both run mostly from 5.9 to 5.12, centred on 5.10 and 5.11, with a decent supply of easier lines and a few harder ones. Walls range from slabs to cracks and featured faces, in single and multi-pitch lengths. Aspects vary, and the Scheelite faces catch morning sun and cool off later in the day. Spring through early fall is the practical window, and the canyon is a cooler retreat from the heat down in town. The largest pockets are Scheelite Canyon, the PSOM Slab, Brownstone Mine and Uptown Rock.

wi_west_bluff.blurb: West Bluff is the hillside above the western shore of Devil's Lake in Wisconsin's Baraboo Range, and it is all bouldering. The problems are on hard quartzite, scattered across an east-facing slope in a series of boulder fields, some open and sunny and others shaded under trees. Landings are uneven talus, so extra pads matter. The grades cover nearly the whole range, from V0 to V10, with most problems between V1 and V5 and a solid band of hard ones in the V7 to V9 range. Fall is the prime time, while summer turns hot and humid and winter snow can end the season. The bluff is split into North, Central, South and Fire Road sections.

ca_queen_valley_area.blurb: Queen Valley is a quieter, more remote corner of Joshua Tree National Park, lying between the park's central and Pinto Basin areas. Trad climbing leads, with bouldering close behind, and only a little sport and top-rope. Roped grades run mostly from 5.8 to 5.11 and cluster around 5.10, while the problems are mainly easy to moderate, with a sprinkling of harder ones. Rock formations are scattered on both sides of the dirt road through the valley, and several of the walk-ins are among the longest anywhere in the park. The three main sub-areas are Geology Tour Road, Queen Mountain and Desert Queen Mine.

nh_wm_waterville_valley.blurb: Waterville Valley sits in the White Mountains of New Hampshire. It was long a quiet backwater and has seen steady development in recent years. Sport and bouldering lead the numbers, with a healthy amount of trad, and roped grades run mostly from 5.8 to 5.12 with a few hard sport lines above. The terrain is varied: sweeping slabs at Dickey Ledge, small forested crags at Bald Knob, roadside sport at Russell Crags, tall alpine cracks on Mount Osceola, and ice in winter. Routes on Welch Mountain are short but high in quality, and there is plenty of untouched rock, with solitude and mountain views.

ca_echo_rock_area.blurb: Echo Rock Area is a cluster of formations and granite corridors in the central part of Joshua Tree National Park, and it is among the park's most popular zones thanks to short walk-ins and a huge number of climbs. Trad is the main event, with a good amount of sport, top-rope and bouldering too. Roped grades run mostly from 5.7 to 5.11, peaking at 5.10, so moderates are plentiful, and there are face and crack lines throughout. Echo Cove has walls facing several ways, so it can be climbed through the year at different times of day. Echo Cove, Echo Rock, Little Hunk and Snickers hold the biggest concentrations.
